source_title: Delta Air Lines, Inc. - Form 10-K and Full-Year 2020 Results (Fiscal Year 2020)
publisher_issuer: Delta Air Lines, Inc. (filed with U.S. SEC, EDGAR CIK 0000027904; corroborated by Delta full-year 2020 earnings release)
company_context: Delta Air Lines is a major U.S. network carrier. COVID-19 collapsed air-travel demand in 2020, turning a record-profit airline into a record-loss one. Delta survived through massive liquidity raising, capacity and cost cuts, and CARES Act payroll support, avoiding bankruptcy.
macro_context: COVID-19 pandemic devastated air travel; the U.S. CARES Act provided airline payroll support and loans, and frequent-flyer-program-backed financing markets enabled large secured debt raises.
evidence_summary: Delta's full-year 2020 operating revenue fell to $17.1 billion from about $47 billion in 2019, and it posted a net loss of about $12.4 billion (versus a $4.8 billion profit in 2019), its worst year ever. To survive, Delta raised large amounts of liquidity, including borrowing $6.5 billion backed by its SkyMiles frequent-flyer program, secured term loans and aircraft sale-leasebacks, and received CARES Act payroll support including a low-interest unsecured government loan. It ended 2020 with about $16.7 billion in liquidity, reduced capacity and costs, and avoided bankruptcy.

source_backed_metrics.cares_act_payroll_support_usd: approximately 5.4 billion (including a ~1.6 billion unsecured 10-year low-interest loan)

owner_decision_context: Facing an unprecedented demand collapse, management chose to maximize liquidity (monetize the loyalty program, take secured debt and sale-leasebacks, accept government payroll support) while cutting capacity, fleet, and costs, rather than risk insolvency, treating the shock as temporary and bridgeable.
action_taken: Raised liquidity including $6.5B of SkyMiles-backed debt, secured term loans, and aircraft sale-leasebacks; accepted ~$5.4B of CARES Act payroll support (incl. a ~$1.6B unsecured government loan); cut capacity, retired aircraft, and reduced costs, ending 2020 with ~$16.7B liquidity.
outcome_evidence: Despite a record ~$12.4B net loss and revenue falling to $17.1B from ~$47B, Delta maintained ~$16.7B liquidity at year-end 2020, avoided bankruptcy, and recovered as travel demand returned, confirming a temporary-shock-with-recovery outcome.
source_limitations: WebFetch of sec.gov and the PR Newswire / Delta IR releases returned 403; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to Delta's full-year 2020 results / 10-K and named journalism (CNN, FlightGlobal, AJC, CNBC, U.S. Treasury): revenue $17.1B vs ~$47B, net loss ~$12.4B vs ~$4.8B profit, $6.5B SkyMiles financing, ~$16.7B year-end liquidity, ~$5.4B CARES support incl. ~$1.6B loan. Exact monthly cash-burn figure not separately confirmed and omitted.
directly_stated: Full-year 2020 operating revenue was $17.1 billion, down from about $47 billion in 2019
Delta reported a net loss of approximately $12.4 billion for 2020, versus a ~$4.8 billion profit in 2019
Delta borrowed $6.5 billion backed by its SkyMiles frequent-flyer program
Delta received approximately $5.4 billion of CARES Act payroll support, including a ~$1.6 billion unsecured 10-year low-interest loan
Delta ended 2020 with approximately $16.7 billion in liquidity
inferred: Delta was a structurally healthy, record-profit airline pushed into severe distress purely by an exogenous demand shock
Loyalty-program monetization plus government support were decisive in bridging the demand trough without bankruptcy
why_useful_for_opsiq: Severe-distress / temporary-shock-with-recovery (outcome 3/13) case of a healthy business hit by a macro demand collapse that responds with a governed liquidity-and-cost playbook (monetize loyalty asset, secured debt, government support, capacity cuts) and recovers. Tests whether the engine classifies the condition as temporary shock requiring liquidity defense and credits asset monetization and cost discipline as phase-correct actions.
